analysis.one_liner: Requires groups spending big money in elections, including corporations and 'dark money' nonprofits, to disclose their donors.
analysis.headline: The DISCLOSE Act of 2021, backed by 200 Democratic cosponsors, never received a committee vote or a floor vote in the House and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would expand the ban on foreign money in elections, covering online political ads, ballot initiatives, and federal judicial nominations. It would require corporations, unions, super PACs, and tax-exempt 'dark money' groups that spend more than $10,000 on election activity to report it to the Federal Election Commission within 24 hours, along with their major funders. Political ads would have to name their top funders on screen or on air, and setting up a shell company to hide foreign election money would become a crime punishable by up to five years in prison.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters. Anyone who sees a political ad would learn within seconds who paid for it, and the FEC would publish who is bankrolling campaign spending within 24 hours of major expenditures. The foreign-money provisions target secret influence by overseas interests in candidate races, ballot measures, and judge nominations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters who want to know who funds ads

how_it_helps.text: Covered organizations — corporations, labor organizations, 501(c) groups, and certain political committees — that spend more than $10,000 in an election cycle must file FEC reports within 24 hours, listing each disbursement over $1,000 and identifying their beneficial owners and funders who gave $10,000 or more.

Political ads not authorized by candidates must carry an 'I approve this message'-style statement from the payer, and video and internet ads must show a list of the payer's top five funders (top two on radio), while also covering prerecorded robocalls.

The foreign-money ban is extended to paid online and digital communications, to ballot initiatives and referenda, and to federal judicial nomination communications; foreign nationals are barred from directing any person's election spending, and CEOs must certify compliance under penalty of perjury.
It becomes a federal crime, punishable by up to five years in prison, to create or use a corporation or other entity with the intent to conceal a foreign national's election contribution.

The FEC must audit each federal election cycle for illicit foreign money and report to Congress, including on disinformation aimed at depressing turnout in rural, minority, and military-veteran communities.

analysis.who_pays: Organizations that spend on elections without currently naming donors — super PACs, 501(c)(4) and 501(c)(6) 'dark money' groups, corporations, and unions — would bear compliance costs and lose donor anonymity. Large online platforms (50 million or more U.S. monthly users) would take on new political-ad disclosure duties. Donors who give $10,000 or more to these groups would appear in public FEC filings.

drawbacks.text: Public donor disclosure can expose givers to harassment or retaliation; the bill recognizes this and carves out an exception allowing names to be omitted when disclosure would subject a person to serious threats, harassment, or reprisals.

The compliance load is real: covered organizations must track, certify, and report disbursements within 24 hours, and CEOs must certify no foreign involvement under penalty of perjury, costs that fall hardest on smaller nonprofits and trade associations.
Unions are covered organizations under the bill, so the same 24-hour disclosure rules and funder lists would apply to labor's political spending, not just to corporate spending.

Supporters of broad political spending rights argue disclosure requirements themselves can burden or chill speech, which is why the bill routes constitutional challenges to a single court (the D.C. district court) with expedited review — a channeling that itself invites objection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is simple: voters learn who is paying for the politics aimed at them, while the groups paying lose anonymity and take on reporting paperwork. The bill tries to blunt the strongest objection — donor harassment — with an explicit exception, and it applies its rules to unions as well as corporations. The design is broad, reaching $10,000-level spending and judicial-nomination ads, so the compliance burden is real; but the main cost falls on the organizations and donors who currently give in secret, not on voters.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in February 2021 and referred to three House committees, then to a Judiciary subcommittee two months later, and no committee ever voted on it or scheduled it for the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David Cicilline introduced the DISCLOSE Act of 2021 on February 25, 2021, with 200 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred the same day to the Committee on House Administration and, in addition, to the Committees on Ways and Means and Judiciary.
On April 28, 2021, it was referred to the Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties of the Judiciary Committee.
No further action was taken: the bill never received a committee markup, a House floor vote, or Senate consideration, and it died at the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023.
Every cosponsor was a Democrat — 200 Democratic cosponsors joined the Democratic sponsor — and no Republican signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Organizations and donors that spend on elections without disclosing their funders are better off: no new reporting, no funder lists on ads, and no expanded foreign-money rules took effect. House Democrats' broader election bills, including a DISCLOSE provision inside the For the People Act, likewise stalled, so the status quo of undisclosed campaign spending continued through the 2022 elections.

industries.industry: 'Dark money' political spenders (super PACs, 501(c)(4) and 501(c)(6) groups)
industries.note: These groups exist in large part to spend on elections without naming donors; the bill would force 24-hour disclosure of big expenditures and public listing of their $10,000-plus funders. Their interest in keeping donor identities hidden runs directly against voters' interest in knowing who pays for ads.

Corporations would have to disclose beneficial owners, report disbursements over $1,000, have their CEO certify no foreign involvement under penalty of perjury, and put top-funder lists on their ads. The bill's rules would reach corporate money precisely where it is currently hardest to trace.

Labor organizations are covered organizations under the bill, so the same 24-hour reporting, certification, and ad-disclaimer rules would apply to union political spending. Unions gain from corporate transparency but bear the same disclosure burden on their own activity.

industries.industry: Large online platforms (50 million or more U.S. monthly users)
industries.note: Social networks, ad networks, and search engines above that threshold would face new obligations around qualified political ads, including rules tied to foreign-money prohibitions on paid online communications. The bill's compliance duties would fall mainly on the biggest platforms.
